claim: More than one out of every seven human couples are infertile.
source: For example, more than one out of every seven human couples are infertile (Thoma et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thoma et al., 2013

claim: Gamete-killing meiotic drive alleles can increase their transmission into up to 100% of the progeny of a heterozygote.
source: These genes act by killing the gametes that do not inherit them, increasing their transmission into up to 100% of the progeny of a heterozygote (Lindholm et al., 2016; Sandler and Novitski, 1957).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lindholm et al., 2016 and Sandler and Novitski, 1957

claim: Gamete-killing meiotic drive has been observed in eukaryotes ranging from plants to mammals.
source: Gamete-killing meiotic drive has been observed in eukaryotes ranging from plants to mammals (Lindholm et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lindholm et al., 2016

claim: Only a handful of genes involved in meiotic drive have been identified.
source: However, only a handful of genes involved in meiotic drive have been identified.
evidence: Statement about the state of knowledge in the field

claim: Schizosaccharomyces pombe strain 972 and Schizosaccharomyces kambucha are 99.5% identical at the nucleotide level.
source: Despite being 99.5% identical at the nucleotide level, Sp/Sk hybrids are nearly sterile (Rhind et al., 2011; Zanders et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Rhind et al., 2011 and Zanders et al., 2014

claim: Sp/Sk hybrids are nearly sterile despite being 99.5% identical at the nucleotide level.
source: Despite being 99.5% identical at the nucleotide level, Sp/Sk hybrids are nearly sterile (Rhind et al., 2011; Zanders et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Rhind et al., 2011 and Zanders et al., 2014

claim: Genes on each of the three Sk chromosomes are capable of enacting gamete-killing meiotic drive against their Sp homologs.
source: Indeed, we previously found that genes on each of the three Sk chromosomes are capable of enacting gamete (spore)-killing meiotic drive against their Sp homologs (Figure 1A) (Zanders et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Zanders et al., 2014) and reference to Figure 1A

claim: Greater than 80% of viable haploid gametes inherit an Sk marker allele from Sk/Sp hybrids on chromosome 3.
source: In this work, we focused on chromosome 3 because it is the smallest chromosome and the drive phenotype is strong: greater than 80% of viable haploid gametes inherit an Sk marker allele from Sk/Sp hybrids (Zanders et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zanders et al., 2014

claim: The Sk drive allele active in diploid 1 is found within a ~30 kb region.
source: We selected diploid 9 for further analysis, as it contains the Sk/Sp mosaic chromosome with the smallest region of Sp-derived DNA (~30 kb) that a pure Sk chromosome can drive against (Figure 1C and Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by genetic mapping data presented in Figure 1C and Figure 1D

claim: The ~30 kb candidate region in Sp contains wtf4 and the wtf3 pseudogene.
source: In Sp, this region contains wtf4 and the wtf3 pseudogene.
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1D

claim: The syntenic region in Sk contains only one wtf gene, wtf4.
source: The syntenic region in Sk contains only one wtf gene, wtf4.
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1D

claim: Sk wtf4 is a member of the wtf gene family that has 25 members in Sp.
source: This gene is a member of the large, rapidly evolving wtf gene family that has 25 members in Sp.
evidence: Statement about gene family membership and size

claim: Sk wtf4 utilizes dual, overlapping transcripts to encode both a gamete-killing poison and an antidote to the poison.
source: wtf4 utilizes dual, overlapping transcripts to encode both a gamete-killing poison and an antidote to the poison.
evidence: Main finding stated in abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript

claim: All gametes are poisoned by wtf4, whereas only those that inherit wtf4 are rescued by the antidote.
source: To enact drive, all gametes are poisoned, whereas only those that inherit wtf4 are rescued by the antidote.
evidence: Mechanistic model supported by experimental data

claim: The ura4 allele from the pure Sk chromosome is transmitted to 87% of the viable gametes produced by diploid 11.
source: We found that the ura4 allele from the pure Sk chromosome is transmitted to 87% of the viable gametes produced by diploid 11, which is not significantly different from the 88% transmission of the Sk allele in diploid 1 (Figure 1C and Figure 2A).
evidence: Experimental data presented in Figure 2A

claim: Only 81% of spores generated by diploid 11 excluded PI, while wild-type strains have rates >90%.
source: We found that only 81% of spores generated by diploid 11 excluded PI, while wild-type strains (e.g. diploid 13) have rates >90% (Figure 2A).
evidence: Experimental data presented in Figure 2A

claim: Deletion of Sk wtf4 significantly increases the number of spores that can exclude PI in diploid 12 compared to diploid 11, from 81% to 96%.
source: We observed a significant increase in the number of spores that could exclude PI in diploid 12 (Sk wtf4Δ), compared to diploid 11 (Sk wtf4+) from 81% to 96%, suggesting Sk wtf4+ promotes spore death in progeny of heterozygous diploids.
evidence: Experimental data presented in Figure 2A

claim: Sk wtf4+ is transmitted to 87% of the viable gametes produced by diploid 11, while the transmission rate of Sk wtf4Δ is reduced to 66% in diploid 12.
source: While Sk wtf4+ is transmitted to 87% of the viable gametes produced by diploid 11, the transmission rate of Sk wtf4Δ is reduced to 66% in diploid 12 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Experimental data presented in Figure 2A

claim: Sk wtf4Δ/Sk wtf4+ heterozygotes in pure Sk background show strong drive (93% transmission) of Sk wtf4+ relative to Sk wtf4Δ.
source: We did, however, observe strong drive (93% transmission) of Sk wtf4+ relative to Sk wtf4Δ in diploid 14 and a concomitant decrease in the percent of spores that could exclude PI (59% versus 92% in wild-type; Figure 2A, diploids 14 and 13).
evidence: Experimental data presented in Figure 2A

claim: The drive of Sk wtf4 does not require an Sp target sequence.
source: These results demonstrate that the drive of Sk wtf4 does not require an Sp target sequence.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data showing drive in pure Sk background

claim: An Sk wtf4Δ homozygote is healthy, with the same ability to exclude PI from the spores as wild-type Sk (92% of spores).
source: Contrary to this expectation, we found that an Sk wtf4Δ homozygote is healthy, with the same ability to exclude PI from the spores as wild-type Sk (92% of spores; Figure 2A, diploids 13 and 15).
evidence: Experimental data presented in Figure 2A

claim: Sk wtf4 does not encode a gene important for meiosis or spore development.
source: This finding rules out the possibility that Sk wtf4 encodes a gene important for meiosis or spore development.
evidence: Conclusion based on the observation that wtf4Δ homozygotes are healthy

claim: Sk wtf4 acts as both poison and antidote, similar to the Spok genes of Podospora anserina.
source: Instead, our results suggest that Sk wtf4 acts as both poison and antidote, similar to the Spok genes of Podospora anserina (Grognet et al., 2014).
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data and comparison to known system

claim: An Sp diploid that is hemizygous for Sk wtf4 (Sk wtf4+/ade6+) produced fewer viable spores (54% PI-excluding spores, versus 96% in the vector-only control).
source: An Sp diploid that is hemizygous for Sk wtf4 (Sk wtf4+/ade6+) produced fewer viable spores (54% PI-excluding spores, versus 96% in the vector-only control) and showed a marked transmission bias (96%) favoring Sk wtf4+ (Figure 2A, diploids 16 and 17).
evidence: Experimental data presented in Figure 2A

claim: An Sp diploid that is hemizygous for Sk wtf4 showed a marked transmission bias (96%) favoring Sk wtf4+.
source: An Sp diploid that is hemizygous for Sk wtf4 (Sk wtf4+/ade6+) produced fewer viable spores (54% PI-excluding spores, versus 96% in the vector-only control) and showed a marked transmission bias (96%) favoring Sk wtf4+ (Figure 2A, diploids 16 and 17).
evidence: Experimental data presented in Figure 2A

claim: Sp diploids homozygous for Sk wtf4+ produced viable spores that excluded PI at the same frequency as spores from wild-type diploids and showed unbiased allele transmission.
source: In contrast, Sp diploids homozygous for Sk wtf4+ produced viable spores that excluded PI at the same frequency as spores from wild-type diploids and showed unbiased allele transmission (Figure 2A, diploids 18 and 16).
evidence: Experimental data presented in Figure 2A

claim: Sk wtf4 acts as a complete one-gene poison-antidote drive system that causes the death of gametes that fail to inherit the locus from heterozygotes.
source: These results are consistent with Sk wtf4 acting as a complete one-gene poison-antidote drive system that causes the death of gametes that fail to inherit the locus from heterozygotes.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data from heterozygous and homozygous diploids

claim: Sp wtf4 is transcribed during meiosis and generates two major overlapping transcripts with different start sites.
source: This revealed that Sp wtf4 is transcribed during meiosis and generates two major overlapping transcripts with different start sites (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on analysis of long-read sequence data from Sp meiotic mRNAs

claim: The region starting 500 bp upstream of the annotated Sp wtf4 start codon until the putative second start codon is 98% identical between Sp and Sk wtf4.
source: Since the region starting 500 bp upstream of the annotated Sp wtf4 start codon until the putative second start codon is fairly well conserved (98% identical) between Sp and Sk wtf4, we hypothesized that Sk wtf4 is likely to produce similar alternate isoforms to Sp wtf4.
evidence: Sequence comparison between Sp and Sk

claim: In Sk Wtf4-GFP/ade6+ heterozygous diploids, faint cytoplasmic Wtf4-GFP signal is observed before the first meiotic division, which intensifies throughout gamete development and fills the ascus surrounding the mature gametes.
source: Visualizing Sk wtf4-GFP/ade6+ heterozygous diploids, we observed faint cytoplasmic Wtf4-GFP signal before the first meiotic division, which intensified throughout gamete development and filled the ascus surrounding the mature gametes (Figure 3C).
evidence: Microscopy data presented in Figure 3C

claim: In mature asci, Wtf4-GFP is strongly enriched within only two of the four spores.
source: In mature asci, we observed a strong enrichment of Wtf4-GFP within only two of the four spores.
evidence: Microscopy data presented in Figure 3C

claim: The surviving PI-negative spores (95% of which inherit Sk wtf4-GFP) are those with the strong Wtf4-GFP signal.
source: Consistent with this idea, we stained asci from Sk wtf4-GFP/ade6+ diploids with PI and observed that the surviving PI-negative spores (95% of which inherit Sk wtf4-GFP) are indeed those with the strong Wtf4-GFP signal (Figure 3D; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Microscopy data presented in Figure 3D and quantitative data in Supplementary file 1

claim: Sk wtf4antidote (with mutated start codon in short transcript) does not cause spore death or transmission bias in hemizygous diploids.
source: In hemizygous diploids (Sk wtf4antidote/ade6+), Sk wtf4antidote does not cause spore death (increased frequency of PI-stained spores) or the transmission bias that is observed with the wild-type Sk wtf4 allele, suggesting that the mutant can no longer drive (compare Figure 4B, diploid 20 to Figure 2A, diploid 17).
evidence: Experimental data presented in Figure 4B

claim: Sk wtf4antidote still protects from meiotic drive since Sk wtf4+/Sk wtf4antidote heterozygotes produce PI-excluding spores at the same frequency as wild-type and show unbiased allele transmission.
source: However, this allele still protects from meiotic drive since Sk wtf4+/Sk wtf4antidote heterozygotes produce PI-excluding spores at the same frequency as wild-type and show unbiased allele transmission (Figure 4B, diploid 21).
evidence: Experimental data presented in Figure 4B

claim: The long transcript of wtf4 has an antidote function.
source: These data assign an antidote function to the long transcript.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data from wtf4antidote mutant

claim: Most spores generated by Sk wtf4poison/ade6+ hemizygotes die (14% exclude PI stain).
source: Indeed, most spores generated by these diploids die (14% exclude PI stain, Figure 4B, diploid 22).
evidence: Experimental data presented in Figure 4B

claim: The Sk wtf4poison allele was modestly underrepresented (38% transmission) in the few surviving spores generated by diploid 22.
source: Interestingly, the Sk wtf4poison allele was modestly underrepresented (38% transmission) in the few surviving spores generated by diploid 22, indicating that the spores that inherit that allele are especially likely to be destroyed by their own poison (Figure 4B).
evidence: Experimental data presented in Figure 4B

claim: In Sk wtf4poison/Sk wtf4+ heterozygotes, spores that inherited the complete Sk wtf4+ gene are immune to Sk wtf4poison toxicity, while those that inherit Sk wtf4poison die.
source: As expected, the spores that inherited the complete Sk wtf4+ gene from these diploids were immune to Sk wtf4poison toxicity, while those that inherit Sk wtf4poison die. (Figure 4B, diploid 23).
evidence: Experimental data presented in Figure 4B

claim: The short Sk wtf4 transcript encodes a trans-acting gamete poison.
source: These results support our model that the short Sk wtf4 transcript encodes a trans-acting gamete poison.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data from wtf4poison mutant

claim: Only 45% of the spores produced by Sk wtf4antidote/Sk wtf4poison heterozygotes can exclude PI stain and 88% of the surviving gametes inherit the Sk wtf4antidote allele.
source: Only 45% of the spores produced by Sk wtf4antidote/Sk wtf4poison heterozygotes can exclude PI stain and 88% of the surviving gametes inherit the Sk wtf4antidote allele (Figure 4B, diploid 24).
evidence: Experimental data presented in Figure 4B

claim: Sk mCherryantidote-wtf4 acts similarly to the wild-type wtf4 allele.
source: To visualize the antidote peptide, we generated an Sk mCherryantidote-wtf4 allele (Figure 5A) and found it acts similarly to the wild-type wtf4 allele (Figure 5B, diploids 25 and 26) (Hailey et al., 2002).
evidence: Experimental data presented in Figure 5B

claim: Sk Wtf4poison-GFP expression is observed before the meiotic divisions and later fills mature asci.
source: In Sk mCherryantidote-wtf4/ Sk wtf4poison-GFP heterozygotes, we observed Sk Wtf4poison-GFP expression before the meiotic divisions and later filling mature asci.
evidence: Microscopy data presented in Figure 5C

claim: Sk mCherryantidote-Wtf4 is enriched only in two of the four mature spores.
source: In contrast, we observe Sk mCherryantidote-Wtf4 enriched only in two of the four mature spores (Figure 5C).
evidence: Microscopy data presented in Figure 5C

claim: Sk wtf28 causes strong drive (90% transmission bias and only 57% of spores excluded PI).
source: However, like Sk wtf4, Sk wtf28 caused strong drive (90% transmission bias and only 57% of spores excluded PI; Figure 2A, diploid 19).
evidence: Experimental data presented in Figure 2A

claim: Sk wtf2 was transmitted to 47% of progeny.
source: Sk wtf2 was transmitted to 47% (n = 114) of progeny
evidence: Experimental data from allele transmission assay

claim: Sk wtf5 was transmitted to 44% of progeny.
source: Sk wtf5 was transmitted to 44% (n = 454)
evidence: Experimental data from allele transmission assay

claim: Sk wtf6 was transmitted to 51% of progeny.
source: Sk wtf6 was transmitted to 51% (n = 471)
evidence: Experimental data from allele transmission assay

claim: The combination of Sk wtf21 and wtf26 was transmitted to 46% of progeny.
source: the combination of Sk wtf21 and wtf26 (cloned and integrated together) was transmitted to 46% (n = 111).
evidence: Experimental data from allele transmission assay

claim: wtf26 and wtf28 are not found in Sp, so have either been lost in Sp, or gained in Sk since divergence.
source: wtf26 and wtf28 are not found in Sp, so have either been lost in Sp, or gained in Sk since divergence.
evidence: Comparative genomic analysis between Sp and Sk

claim: Sk wtf2 is a 1036 bp full length gene, while Sp wtf2 is likely a 388 bp pseudogene.
source: While Sk wtf2 is a 1036 bp full length gene, Sp wtf2 is likely a 388 bp pseudogene (it has a large deletion relative to other wtf genes and multiple in-frame stop codons).
evidence: Sequence analysis of wtf2 in both species

claim: Sk wtf21 is likely a pseudogene, whereas Sp wtf21 is intact.
source: Sk wtf21 is likely a pseudogene (multiple in frame stop codons), whereas Sp wtf21 is intact.
evidence: Sequence analysis of wtf21 in both species

claim: Sp and Sk wtf21 loci share 83% DNA sequence identity.
source: The two loci share 83% DNA sequence identity.
evidence: Sequence comparison between Sp and Sk wtf21

claim: The wtf5 gene is intact in both Sp and Sk species, and the loci share 99% DNA sequence identity and 97% amino acid identity.
source: The wtf5 gene is intact in both species, and the loci share 99% DNA sequence identity and 97% amino acid identity.
evidence: Sequence comparison between Sp and Sk wtf5

claim: Sp and Sk wtf6 share 82% nucleotide identity, but only 74% amino acid identity.
source: Sp and Sk wtf6 share 82% nucleotide identity, but only 74% amino acid identity.
evidence: Sequence comparison between Sp and Sk wtf6

claim: The wtf loci show much greater sequence divergence than the 99.5% genome average identity between Sp and Sk.
source: Altogether, the wtf loci show much greater sequence divergence than the 99.5% genome average identity between Sp and Sk.
evidence: Comparison of wtf loci divergence to genome-wide average

claim: Rapid evolution is a hallmark of genes involved in genetic conflicts, such as loci involved in causing or suppressing meiotic drive.
source: Such rapid evolution is a hallmark of genes involved in genetic conflicts, such as loci involved in causing or suppressing meiotic drive (Daugherty and Malik, 2012; McLaughlin and Malik, 2017; Henikoff et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Daugherty and Malik, 2012; McLaughlin and Malik, 2017; Henikoff et al., 2001

claim: Sk wtf28 is the only one of the six genes tested that has a putative alternate start codon in exon two that could be used to make a putative short poison isoform.
source: Intriguingly, the Sk wtf28 drive gene is also the only one of the six genes we tested that also has a putative alternate start codon in exon two that could be used to make a putative short poison isoform.
evidence: Sequence analysis of tested wtf genes

claim: Hu et al., 2017 identified two different wtf drivers in another Sp isolate (CBS5557) and both have a potential alternate start codon in exon 2.
source: Additionally, Hu et al., 2017 also identified two different wtf drivers in another Sp isolate (CBS5557) and both have a potential alternate start codon in exon 2.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hu et al., 2017

claim: Of the 25 wtf loci in Sp, four (wtf4, wtf13, wtf19 and wtf23) appear to be capable of encoding two proteins and are predicted to be active drive genes.
source: Of the 25 wtf loci in Sp, four (wtf4, wtf13, wtf19 and wtf23) also appear to be capable of encoding two proteins and we predict these are active drive genes.
evidence: Sequence analysis and prediction based on structural features

claim: The intact genes tested that did not confer drive (Sk wtf2, wtf5, wtf6, and wtf26) all encode genes similar to the antidote isoform of Sk wtf4 but appear to lack a shorter poison isoform.
source: In contrast, the intact genes we tested that did not confer drive, Sk wtf2, wtf5, wtf6, and wtf26, all encode genes similar to the antidote isoform of Sk wtf4 but appear to lack a shorter poison isoform.
evidence: Sequence analysis and comparison to wtf4 structure

claim: The ancestral function of the wtf family is to confer meiotic drive.
source: Together, our results and those of Hu et al., 2017) are consistent with the hypothesis that the ancestral function of the wtf family is to confer meiotic drive.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data and comparison to other studies

claim: Sk wtf4 is a novel, gamete-killing meiotic drive locus.
source: Our study demonstrates that Sk wtf4 is a novel, gamete-killing meiotic drive locus.
evidence: Summary of main finding supported by all experimental data

claim: Like the Spok family of drivers found in Podospora, wtf4 is an autonomous drive system that confers both the ability to kill gametes that do not inherit the gene and the ability to protect the gametes that do.
source: Like the Spok family of drivers found in Podospora, wtf4 is an autonomous drive system that confers both the ability to kill gametes that do not inherit the gene and the ability to protect the gametes that do (Grognet et al., 2014).
evidence: Comparison to known system supported by citation to Grognet et al., 2014

claim: wtf4 achieves poison and antidote functions by a previously undescribed mechanism in which the gene encodes a poison protein from one transcriptional start site and an antidote protein from an alternative transcriptional start site.
source: We show that wtf4 achieves these disparate functions by a previously undescribed mechanism in which the gene encodes a poison protein from one transcriptional start site and an antidote protein from an alternative transcriptional start site.
evidence: Summary of mechanistic finding supported by experimental data

claim: The poison protein is trans-acting and has the capacity to destroy all gametes, but the antidote remains in the gametes that inherit the wtf4 locus and specifically rescues them from destruction.
source: We show that the poison protein is trans-acting and has the capacity to destroy all gametes, but that the antidote remains in the gametes that inherit the wtf4 locus and specifically rescues them from destruction.
evidence: Summary of mechanistic finding supported by localization and functional data

claim: The poison-antidote mechanism of Sk wtf4 is comparable to bacterial toxin-antitoxin (TA) systems.
source: The poison-antidote mechanism of Sk wtf4 is comparable to the bacterial toxin-antitoxin (TA) systems.
evidence: Comparison to known biological systems

claim: TA systems are found in most prokaryotes and have been extensively studied.
source: These systems are found in most prokaryotes and have been extensively studied.
evidence: Statement about established knowledge

claim: Outside of its role in meiotic drive, wtf4 has no apparent role in promoting fertility.
source: Outside of its role in meiotic drive, wtf4 has no apparent role in promoting fertility (Figure 2A, diploid 15).
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data showing wtf4Δ homozygotes are healthy

claim: The wild-type allele of wtf4 causes infertility to promote its own fitness.
source: In other words, the wild-type allele of wtf4 causes infertility to promote its own fitness.
evidence: Interpretation of the selfish nature of wtf4 based on experimental data

claim: wtf4 is in a state of genetic conflict with the rest of the genome because infertility is clearly bad for fitness of loci unlinked to wtf4.
source: This puts wtf4 into a state of genetic conflict with the rest of the genome because infertility is clearly bad for fitness of loci unlinked to wtf4.
evidence: Logical inference about evolutionary dynamics

claim: The DNA sequence divergence between Sk and Sp at the wtf4 locus is more than 20-fold higher than the genome-wide average.
source: Consistent with the idea that the gene is locked in such an arms race, the DNA sequence divergence between Sk and Sp at the wtf4 locus is more than 20-fold higher than the genome-wide average (Rhind et al., 2011; Zanders et al., 2014).
evidence: Sequence comparison data supported by citations

claim: The coding sequence overlap between the poison and antidote could promote specificity between the two components.
source: We propose, however, that the coding sequence overlap between the poison and antidote could promote specificity between the two components, for example, by the antidote acting as a dominant suppressor of the poison.
evidence: Proposed model based on structural features

claim: Using a shared sequence to confer specificity between drive components may be a recurring theme amongst gamete-killers.
source: In this manner, the poison could diverge without losing the self-protection conferred by the antidote. Using a shared sequence to confer specificity between drive components may be a recurring theme amongst gamete-killers.
evidence: Speculation based on comparison to other systems

claim: There are >20 wtf loci on Sp (and likely Sk) chromosome 3 that could contribute to the complex drive phenotypes observed.
source: For example, there are >20 wtf loci on Sp (and likely Sk) chromosome 3 that could contribute to the complex drive phenotypes we observe (Figure 1) (Bowen et al., 2003).
evidence: Genomic data supported by citation to Bowen et al., 2003

claim: Different wtf genes represent distinct evolutionary stages.
source: We propose that different wtf genes represent distinct evolutionary stages.
evidence: Proposed evolutionary model based on functional and sequence data

claim: The putative ancestral type wtf genes (Sk wtf4 and wtf28) are still active as meiotic drivers and encode both poison and antidote proteins.
source: The putative ancestral type (Sk wtf4 and wtf28) are still active as meiotic drivers and encode both poison and antidote proteins.
evidence: Classification based on functional and structural data

claim: There are 25 wtf loci in the Sp genome.
source: There are 25 wtf loci in the Sp genome and this work combined with that of Hu and colleagues implicates these genes in causing and/or modifying meiotic drive (Bowen et al., 2003; Hu et al., 2017 ).
evidence: Genomic data supported by citations

claim: Meiotic drive has played a significant role in the evolution of the Sp group of fission yeasts, despite the heavy fitness costs these selfish loci can levy.
source: Meiotic drive has therefore played a significant role in the evolution of the Sp group of fission yeasts, despite the heavy fitness costs these selfish loci can levy.
evidence: Conclusion based on the prevalence of wtf genes and their drive functions

claim: Sk and Sp have different karyotypes on chromosomes 2 and 3 due to a translocation.
source: Because Sp and Sk have different karyotypes on chromosomes 2 and 3 due to a translocation (Zanders et al., 2014), we could not generate such a strain as it would lack essential genes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zanders et al., 2014

claim: Sk wtf4 shares only 89% DNA sequence identity (82% amino acid identity) with the gene in the orthologous locus in Sp.
source: Sk wtf4 shares only 89% DNA sequence identity (82% amino acid identity) with the gene in the orthologous locus in Sp (Sp wtf4); this divergence is much higher than expected given the 99.5% average DNA sequence identity between the two genomes (Rhind et al., 2011; Zanders et al., 2014).
evidence: Sequence comparison data supported by citations

claim: Sk wtf4 is a 1427 bp gene (from the start to stop codon, including introns) with six exons.
source: Sk wtf4 is a 1427 bp gene (from the start to stop codon, including introns) with six exons and encodes a protein with six predicted transmembrane domains.
evidence: Sequence analysis of Sk wtf4

claim: Sk wtf4 encodes a protein with six predicted transmembrane domains.
source: Sk wtf4 is a 1427 bp gene (from the start to stop codon, including introns) with six exons and encodes a protein with six predicted transmembrane domains.
evidence: Computational prediction based on sequence

claim: wtf genes are transcribed during meiosis.
source: We reasoned that wtf genes, in general, were good candidates for meiotic drive loci because of their rapid evolution and their transcription during meiosis (Bowen et al., 2003; Mata et al., 2002; Daugherty and Malik, 2012; McLaughlin and Malik, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bowen et al., 2003 and Mata et al., 2002

claim: wtf genes are rapidly evolving.
source: We reasoned that wtf genes, in general, were good candidates for meiotic drive loci because of their rapid evolution and their transcription during meiosis (Bowen et al., 2003; Mata et al., 2002; Daugherty and Malik, 2012; McLaughlin and Malik, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Daugherty and Malik, 2012 and McLaughlin and Malik, 2017

claim: The infertility of Sp/Sk hybrids is caused by both chromosomal rearrangements and multiple meiotic drivers.
source: In the case of Sp/Sk hybrids (and likely other pairings), the infertility is caused by both chromosomal rearrangements and multiple meiotic drivers (Zanders et al., 2014; Avelar et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zanders et al., 2014 and Avelar et al., 2013

claim: The rapid evolution of infertility is common amongst fission yeasts that are generally categorized as isolates of the Schizosaccharomyces pombe species.
source: This rapid evolution of infertility is common amongst fission yeasts that are generally categorized as isolates of the Schizosaccharomyces pombe species (Avelar et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Avelar et al., 2013

claim: A reproductive barrier between Sp and Sk must have arisen very recently.
source: Despite being 99.5% identical at the nucleotide level, Sp/Sk hybrids are nearly sterile (Rhind et al., 2011; Zanders et al., 2014); a reproductive barrier between these yeasts must have arisen very recently.
evidence: Inference based on high sequence identity and sterility
